content:
Well now. You want Thunderbird to tell your browser of choice (whatever that might be) that it should open links in a private window. Despite your choice being Firefox the underlying assumption is the browser is decided by operating system settings, not Thunderbird. It just passes HTTPS requests to the operating system for execution.

In the case of Firefox it has a right click menu but you issue is you want to tell Windows 10 that it should open links in Firefox using a private window.

Generally there are two way to do that. Only the first applies in this situation.

If you want Firefox to always run in Private Browsing mode by default: • Permanent Setting: Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > scroll to History > choose “Never remember history” from the drop-down menu and restart Firefox. • Shortcut Flag (Windows): Right-click your Firefox desktop shortcut, select Properties, and add -private-window to the end of the target path inside the Target field

Thunderbird has a similar issue to what you want with oAuth and Yahoo. Yahoo shares cookies when setting up oAuth and Thunderbird was unable to offload that to the browser because there is not way to tell the browser to open a private window this time. Every other provider now authenticates using the system browser except Yahoo.

If the developers can not achieve it for their authentication needs, I think your chances are slim beyond making it a permanent setting in the browser.

There are some hidden preferences relating to helper applications that might be made to setup a non system browser to execute HTTPS requests, but it is not tested and the preferences exist primarily for Linux but I think they could be bent out of shape to fit. I certainly do not have the interest to experiment with them however. See https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/hyperlinks-in-messages-not-working

Nothing has really changed since this 2016 discussion https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/questions/1111028

content:
I actually doubt the issue is Thunderbird on the face of it. Despite it being the one exhibiting the problem.

First most issues with mail come from security software these days, not failure with the mail client or the mail provider. Multiple copies of the same message on a POP mail account usually mean a defective mail scanning component. I first observer it with Norton a decade or more ago. Since that time the issue has actually become worse with more antivirus product involved. Essentially what happens is;

  • Thunderbird attempt to get mail.
  • The antivirus sticks its nose in to scan the email. This in not in a friendly way. Often the antivirus actually pretends to be the mail server as far as Thunderbird is concerned and pretends to be a mail client as far as the server is concerned. Like a spider in it's web it sits there.
  • Along comes a malformed email that causes the antivirus pt choke and die.
  • Now Thunderbird has lost its connection to the server because of the fake server. The server sits waiting for a response and eventually times out.

This is bad enough, but Thunderbird only updates its internal "where are we up to" information at the end of a POP mail session so the timeout causes Thunderbird to simply reset.

In 10 minutes or so, or sooner is someone pushed the get mail button the whole circus kicks off again, the same email get downloaded the same email causes he premature death of the AV product and again everything resets. AN email version of groundhog day really.

Now what to do;

  1. My personal choice years ago was to simply abandon the time wasting involved in mail scanning. It I get an email with a virus the antivirus will pick it up in memory or on disk when I save the attachment or even when I try and open it. (that is one of the reasons Microsoft defender doe not scan incoming or outgoing email)
  2. A more labour intensive approach is start deleting mail in webmail around the time of the last message you received. Because the email is malformed, it is usually to be found in the spam folder. But there is no real way to determine which mail kills the antivirus mail scanning component. It is trial and error
  3. The easiest is turn off mail scanning until you clear all your backlog mail and then you can re-enable scanning again until next time.

For obvious reason I favour my preferred approach because it is never an issue and I have to do nothing nor even really look out for it happening.

The next issue is that your disk may even be actually full but lets try and work out the cause before trying a solution that may not be needed.

I have assumed you use POP to retrieve your mail. If that is in error please say so and post the troubleshooting information from the help menu. to a reply in the forum.
